facts.fact_text: On 29 November 2019 a demonstration was held in front of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia.

The demonstration on 29 November 2019 was part of a series of protests about the Parliament of Georgia's failure to adopt amendments to the Constitution of Georgia meant to facilitate the transition of the parliamentary electoral system from a 'mixed-member' system to one of proportional representation (see Makarashvili and Others v. Georgia, nos. 23158/20 and 2 others, §§ 5-6, 1 September 2022).
The demonstration on 29 November 2019 was attended by opposition politicians, civil society activists and ordinary citizens.

The location of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 in front of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia was apparently chosen because the Minister of Justice had been scheduled to give a speech there.
The exact number of participants in the demonstration on 29 November 2019 remains unclear.
Video material relating to the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows a couple of hundred individuals gathered at the site.
Video material relating to the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows a large number of police officers gathered at the site.
The Minister of Justice entered the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia with the help of a police cordon on 29 November 2019.

Video coverage of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows that the demonstrators attempted several times to break through the police cordon and force their way to the entrance of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia while the Minister of Justice was there.

Video coverage of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows that the pavement and narrow road leading to the entrance of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia were largely occupied by people who had gathered at the demonstration, including police officers.

Footage from the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows the police telling the demonstrators that their actions were contrary to the law and that they could not block the entrance to the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia or the road.
Footage from the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows some demonstrators yelling inaudible phrases at the police officers while the officers remained calm.
Six individuals, including the applicant, were arrested on 29 November 2019 on various grounds.

At some point during the demonstration on 29 November 2019, the applicant turned towards the police officers, allegedly in response to the police calls to clear the road, holding beans in his hand and shouting loudly that beans used to be 'gruel for slaves'.
According to the case file, the applicant then threw the beans at the police officers, crying out 'slave gruel for the police'.
The video footage available in the case file shows that the applicant was arrested immediately after throwing beans at the police officers.
Six individuals, including the applicant, were arrested on 29 November 2019 on various grounds.
It does not appear that the demonstration on 29 November 2019 was dispersed.

At some point during the demonstration on 29 November 2019, the applicant turned towards the police officers, allegedly in response to the police calls to clear the road, holding beans in his hand and shouting loudly that beans used to be 'gruel for slaves'.
According to the case file, the applicant then threw the beans at the police officers, crying out 'slave gruel for the police'.
The video footage available in the case file shows that the applicant was arrested immediately after throwing beans at the police officers.
The applicant's arrest took place at 11.45 a.m. on 29 November 2019.
The applicant was escorted to the Tbilisi police station for having allegedly committed offences under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disorderly conduct/minor hooliganism).

The applicant was escorted to the Tbilisi police station for having allegedly committed offences under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disobeying lawful orders of a law-enforcement officer/insulting a law-enforcement officer).
According to the administrative-offence report, the applicant had blocked the road on 29 November 2019.
According to the administrative-offence report, the applicant had breached public order on 29 November 2019.
According to the administrative-offence report, the applicant had resisted the police on 29 November 2019.
According to the administrative-offence report, the applicant had insulted the police officers on 29 November 2019.
According to the administrative-offence report, the applicant had disobeyed the lawful orders of the police officers on 29 November 2019.
The administrative-arrest report indicated Articles 166 and 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences as the provisions relevant to the applicant's arrest.
The administrative-arrest report stated that on 29 November 2019 the applicant (Lasha Chkhartishvili) blocked the road beside the Public Library located on Purtseladze Street in Tbilisi.
The administrative-arrest report stated that the applicant insulted and harassed members of the public.

The administrative-arrest report stated that despite multiple instructions to stop, the applicant continued in defiance of the law and after the police had ordered him to desist he became more aggressive and threw dried beans at the police officers.
The administrative-arrest report stated that the applicant insulted the police officers and called them slaves.
The administrative-arrest report stated that the applicant was arrested for minor hooliganism and disobeying police orders.
On 29 November 2019 the applicant was brought before the Tbilisi City Court.
The trial before the Tbilisi City Court started at 3.32 p.m. on 29 November 2019.
At the outset of the trial before the Tbilisi City Court, the parties were warned that they must observe order and comply with judicial instructions.
At the outset of the trial before the Tbilisi City Court, the parties were warned that contempt of court would entail sanctions.
The applicant requested the recusal of the judge presiding over his administrative-offence case at the Tbilisi City Court.
The applicant stated that it was always that judge who presided over administrative-offence cases relating to arrests at demonstrations.
The applicant stated that his case had been scheduled for immediate consideration while older administrative-offence cases had still been pending.
The applicant expressed the opinion that the judge was biased and must have been following instructions coming from outside the courtroom.
The judge responded that the applicant's recusal request was unsubstantiated as it did not demonstrate the existence of any grounds provided for by the law for his recusal.
The judge stated that he was on duty that day, which had been the reason for the applicant's case having been assigned to him.
While the judge was speaking, the applicant interrupted in a louder voice, repeating that all politically sensitive cases had been assigned to that judge.
The judge asked the applicant to calm down, to show respect towards the court and to allow the case to proceed.
The applicant responded that he was calm and that it was the judge who had to worry because he would be held accountable before the law for all the politically motivated prosecutions.
The judge explained that he was not interested in any political party, to which the applicant responded: 'we can see that'.
The judge asked the applicant to calm down, warning that failing to do so would result in his removal from the courtroom and the trial proceeding without his attendance or participation.
The applicant repeated that the judge would be held accountable before the law.
The applicant received a fine of 300 Georgian laris (approximately 120 euros) for the offence of contempt of court.
The applicant was notified that the contempt of court fine decision could be appealed against.
The applicant continued, in a calm voice, to accuse the judge of wrongdoing, interrupting him.
The applicant was warned that continued disorderly conduct would result in his removal from the courtroom.
The applicant replied 'remove me, no problem' and made some inaudible remark.
The judge ordered the applicant's removal from the courtroom.

In response to the judge's order for removal, the applicant started yelling that 'slaves' of B.I. (the chairman of Georgian Dream, a political party that at the time in question held an absolute majority in Parliament), like the judge in question, would end up in prison.
The applicant was removed from the courtroom.

After the applicant's removal from the courtroom, the judge stated that, unlike the other cases the applicant had referred to, the applicant's case had involved the element of administrative arrest, rendering the consideration of the case a matter of urgent priority.
The judge continued to hear the administrative-offence case in the applicant's absence.
The applicant's defence lawyer requested that the trial be adjourned, stating that she needed time to familiarise herself with the administrative case file and to collect the evidence.
The applicant's defence lawyer stated that she had not been able to meet with the applicant prior to the trial.
The applicant's defence lawyer alleged that the police had concealed the applicant's whereabouts until his eventual transfer to the courtroom.
The judge granted the adjournment request and adjourned the hearing for three hours and ten minutes.

In response to the complaint that the police had obstructed the lawyer's attempts to meet with the applicant, the lawyer was told that a separate complaint should have been lodged if she believed that the authorities had committed any unlawful actions.
Once the hearing resumed, the applicant's defence lawyer requested that the applicant be questioned as a witness, since she had not had time to consult him.

Once the hearing resumed, the applicant's defence lawyer requested that the trial be postponed again, as she needed additional time to obtain some video recordings in respect of the events complained of.
Once the hearing resumed, the applicant's defence lawyer requested that the applicant be released from detention.
The applicant's defence lawyer complained that the police had exceeded their powers during the applicant's arrest.

The trial judge rejected the application for the applicant to be questioned as a witness, reasoning that the applicant's own behaviour had caused his removal from the courtroom after unheeded warnings and that his appearance as a witness was not justified in such circumstances.

As regards the video evidence which the applicant's defence lawyer had sought to obtain, the trial judge noted that this material had been widely disseminated by the media and the lawyer was free to show those recordings to the court in addition to the material already available in the case file, without the need for further adjournment.
The trial judge noted that the applicant's detention meant that the conduct of the trial had to be especially expeditious, and another adjournment was therefore not considered necessary.
During the hearing before the trial court, the author of the administrative-offence report stated that the applicant had a history of committing administrative offences and disobeying police orders.
During the hearing before the trial court, it was noted that on at least two previous occasions — in 2008 and 2014 — the applicant had been ordered to pay administrative fines.
The author of the administrative-offence report requested, in view of the applicant's history of administrative offences, that the trial court apply a stricter sanction as a deterrent for the future.
The applicant's representative contested the officer's submission regarding the applicant's history of administrative offences as unsubstantiated, unclear and irrelevant.
On 29 November 2019 the Tbilisi City Court acquitted the applicant of any offence under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disorderly conduct/minor hooliganism).

On 29 November 2019 the Tbilisi City Court found the applicant guilty of insulting law-enforcement officers and disobeying their lawful orders, in breach of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court sentenced the applicant to eight days' administrative detention.
The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on the administrative-offence and arrest reports of 29 November 2019.
The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on internal reports of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on a document entitled 'information regarding the accused', reflecting the fact that the applicant had been charged with administrative offences in the past.
The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on the parties' submissions.
The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on witness statements, including the officers' explanation that beans had been thrown in their faces.
The Tbilisi City Court's judgment was based on the video footage relating to the applicant's arrest.

The Tbilisi City Court articulated the view that statements of police officers would, in principle, be sufficient to shift the burden of proof onto a person accused of committing an administrative offence, because of the expertise of the police and the fact that they carried out their professional duties in line with the domestic legislation.

The Tbilisi City Court noted that statements by persons alleged to have breached administrative rules and regulations could not, unless supported by other evidence, be regarded as constituting irrefutable evidence in respect of determining the circumstances of a case, given that the individuals in question were interested parties and that information provided by them could be aimed at covering up an offence and avoiding sanctions.

The Tbilisi City Court established that the case file material confirmed that the applicant showed disobedience towards the lawful demands of the police and insulted the police officers, conduct falling within the scope of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Tbilisi City Court found that there was no evidence which could incontrovertibly confirm the commission of conduct contrary to Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences; namely, the facts of cursing at the site of a public gathering and of a breach of public order had not been established.

The Tbilisi City Court noted that on 29 November 2019 a demonstration was being held along the site of the public library in Tbilisi, on Purtseladze Street, and that police officers were ensuring the peaceful conduct of the demonstration and the implementation of the constitutionally guaranteed rights of citizens.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the police officers were enforcing security, protecting the rights of the participants in the demonstration and ensuring citizens' constitutionally guaranteed right to freely move along Rustaveli Avenue and the adjacent streets, which constituted sufficient grounds for the officers to implement appropriate measures provided for by law.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the evidence, the parties' explanations and the video material confirmed the police officers' instructions and the applicant's disobedience to such instructions, as well as the fact of his insulting the officers.
The Tbilisi City Court found that the law-enforcement authority called on the applicant to leave the road and that request was left unheeded.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the law-enforcement authorities gave instructions to preserve order and that the instructions were lawful and aimed at achieving the legitimate goal of safeguarding individuals and public order.

The Tbilisi City Court found that calling the police officers 'slaves' amounted to behaviour which insulted and degraded the honour and dignity of the police officers and constituted a sufficient basis for the applicant's actions to fall within the scope of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Tbilisi City Court referred to the Freedom of Speech Act, which accepts and protects the freedoms of speech and expression as eternal and supreme human values, while section 8 of the same Act provides for grounds for limiting these freedoms only if such limitations are provided for by law in a clear and foreseeable manner and when the advantage achieved by a limitation exceeds the damage inflicted by it.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the evidence, the parties' submissions and the video material confirmed that the applicant called the police officers 'slaves' and threw beans at them, stating that it had been gruel for slaves.
The Tbilisi City Court noted that section 48(3) of the Police Act provides that insulting the honour and dignity of police officers who are on duty will incur liability under Georgian legislation.

The Tbilisi City Court noted that Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences expressly defines liability for disobeying the lawful orders of police officers on duty, verbally insulting them and/or carrying out insulting actions towards them.

The Tbilisi City Court considered that actions insulting the dignity of police officers — calling them 'slaves' and throwing beans at them while noting that beans used to be gruel for slaves — cannot be considered a form of protest.

The Tbilisi City Court referred to section 111(1) of the Assemblies and Demonstrations Act, which authorises the police to clear the road in the event of the partial or full blocking of a road by the participants in an assembly or a demonstration if the number of the participants allows the holding of those events without blocking the road.

The Tbilisi City Court found that a need to block the road had not been demonstrated in the present case and accordingly the applicant did not have a right to occupy it, and the police officers' repeated requests to have the road cleared to allow cars to circulate were lawful but not complied with.

As regards the sanction of the eight-day custodial sentence imposed on the applicant, the Tbilisi City Court cited Articles 33 and 35 of the Code of Administrative Offences and reasoned that 'in view of the applicant's personality and the degree of seriousness of his actions', the imposition of a fine or a verbal reprimand would not ensure the attainment of the objectives of punishment.
On 1 December 2019 the applicant lodged an appeal against the Tbilisi City Court's decision.

In his appeal, the applicant complained that the trial court had relied exclusively on the police officers' account and that any doubt should have benefited him, according to the principles applicable in criminal proceedings.
In his appeal, the applicant stated that it remained unclear what lawful orders he had disobeyed.

In his appeal, the applicant noted that in circumstances where the trial court had acquitted him of the charge under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, his arrest and conviction for the breach of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences had been devoid of justification.
In his appeal, the applicant submitted that it had been the police who had blocked the road and that he physically could not have blocked it.
In his appeal, the applicant submitted that he had not insulted the police officers.

In his appeal, the applicant stated that he had been unable to meet with his lawyer before the court hearing despite the lawyer's attempt to secure a meeting through the bailiff of the court, though no evidence appears to have been presented on that account.
The applicant did not complain about his removal from the courtroom in his appeal.
On 2 December 2019 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal issued a final decision rejecting the applicant's appeal as inadmissible.
The final decision of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal was served on the applicant on 19 December 2019.
The Tbilisi Court of Appeal found that the parties to the proceedings had been given the opportunity to argue their case and the trial court had correctly assessed all the relevant evidence.

The Tbilisi Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's findings, stating that the applicant had not adduced any evidence or referred to newly discovered circumstances surrounding his administrative-offence case which would have warranted the re-examination of his case on the merits.
Section 9(3) of the Assemblies and Demonstrations Act provides that the blocking of entrances to buildings during an assembly or a demonstration shall be prohibited.
Section 11(2)(e) of the Assemblies and Demonstrations Act provides that it is prohibited to deliberately obstruct traffic.

Section 111 of the Assemblies and Demonstrations Act provides that in the event of participants in a demonstration partially or completely blocking a road used by cars, the police have the right to decide to clear the road and/or restore the movement of vehicles if blocking the road 'is not made necessary by the number of participants in an assembly or a demonstration'.

Article 33 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that the nature of the offence, the personalities of the offenders, the degree of blame to be ascribed to the offenders, their financial status and any extenuating and aggravating circumstances are to be taken into account at the sentencing stage.

Article 35 §§ 1 and 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences lists, among the possible aggravating circumstances to be taken into account at the sentencing stage, 'the continuation of unlawful conduct in the face of demands by authorised officials to cease'.

Article 35 §§ 1 and 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences lists, among the possible aggravating circumstances to be taken into account at the sentencing stage, 'the commission of a similar offence during the year following conviction for an administrative offence or the commission of an offence by an individual who had previously been convicted of a crime'.

Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as worded at the material time, defined disorderly conduct ('minor hooliganism') as 'swearing and cursing in a public place, causing harassment of a person by means of insults, or other similar actions that disturb public order and peace'.

Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as worded at the material time, provided that disorderly conduct ('minor hooliganism') was punishable by a fine and/or up to fifteen days' administrative detention.

Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as worded at the material time, provided that 'disobeying a lawful instruction or order issued by a law-enforcement officer on duty or insulting the latter' was punishable by a fine of a minimum of 1,000 Georgian laris and a maximum of 4,000 Georgian laris, or up to fifteen days' administrative detention.
